surface_forms: Madame la duchesse de La Rochefoucauld

appraisal_events.evidence: « ajoutait Mme de Villeparisis oubliant qu'elle ne comprenait pas ce genre de nuances »; « J'admets que nous l'emportons par les alliances et l'illustration, mais l'ancienneté est presque la même »; later, « telle phrase que Mme de Villeparisis avait dite et dans laquelle se marquait la femme qui tenait plus à sa naissance qu'elle ne l'avouait ».
appraisal_events.explanation: While Mme de Villeparisis tells her anecdote as though genealogical precedence were an antiquated absurdity she cannot follow, the narrator's aside catches her expertly ranking the Choiseul against her own house, and he later names the gap explicitly: she cares about her birth more than she admits. The passage undercuts the very self-effacement that made her charming.

appraisal_events.evidence: « je ne savais jamais le degré d'estime dû à quelqu'un que quand elle me l'avait indiqué »; « les croquis que j'avais pris dans la journée d'après tous ces êtres inexistants qui n'étaient pas elle »; « Sans toi je ne pourrais pas vivre. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Against the whole gallery of Balbec society, the grandmother is set apart as the only real being and as the sole authority licensing the narrator's judgments of everyone else. The elevation is stated in the narrator's own voice and sealed by his declaration that he could not live without her.

status_effects.explanation: Her tact and self-effacement are locally devalued as she is caught prizing her lineage while professing not to understand such distinctions.
She is the arbiter of the narrator's evaluations: he submits his daily sketches of people to her and cannot fix anyone's worth until she has ruled on it.
The narrator's « Sans toi je ne pourrais pas vivre » gives her total emotional leverage, which she then uses to counsel him toward a harder heart.

The obverse of the grandmother's elevation is his avowed dependence, framed by his own diagnosis of « nervosisme » and a « penchant maladif à la tristesse » and by his heart tightening at the mere idea of her absence.

ambiguities: The grandmother's praise of Mme de Villeparisis (« elle me vantait Mme de Villeparisis ») pulls against E1, but the narrator immediately reattributes that praise to an instinctive concern for his own fragile happiness rather than to Mme de Villeparisis's merits, so it does not offset the diminishment.

Within the anecdote, the mockery of the duchesse de La Rochefoucauld's bulk and the appraisal of her husband's false judgment are evaluations made by Mme de Villeparisis's mother and quoted at two removes; they characterize the teller's milieu rather than register as local status movement for those figures, so no event is recorded for them.
